title: Windows Servers: The PowerShell You Need
intro: Plenty of estates include Windows servers: .NET applications on IIS, SQL Server, Active Directory. The troubleshooting questions are the ones you know from Linux; the tool is PowerShell. Its commands are verb-noun pairs, and they pass objects down a pipeline, not text, so you filter on properties instead of parsing columns. You're in a PowerShell session on a web server.

steps.prompt: Check the state of the IIS web service, whose service name is W3SVC.
steps.fake_output:
Status   Name               DisplayName
------   ----               -----------
Stopped  W3SVC              World Wide Web Publishing Service
steps.why: Get-Service is 'systemctl status'. Cmdlet names follow Verb-Noun, so they can be guessed: Get-, Start-, Stop-, Restart-Service. 'Get-Command *service*' finds them and 'Get-Help <name> -Examples' is the manual page.

steps.prompt: Find out why. Show the 20 newest errors in the System event log.
steps.fake_output:
Index Time          EntryType   Source                 InstanceID Message
----- ----          ---------   ------                 ---------- -------
88120 Oct 02 14:02  Error       Service Control Manager      7023 The World Wide Web Publishing Service service terminated with the following error: The dependency service or group failed to start.
88119 Oct 02 14:02  Error       Service Control Manager      7001 The Windows Process Activation Service depends on the following service: the Net.Pipe Listener Adapter failed to start.
88104 Oct 02 14:01  Error       Microsoft-Windows-WAS        5005 Windows Process Activation Service (WAS) is stopping because it encountered an error. The data field contains the error number.
steps.explanation: IIS stopped because a service it depends on, Windows Process Activation, failed.
steps.why: The event log is Windows's journal: System for the operating system and services, Application for programs, Security for logons and audit. Read upward from the symptom to the first failure, as with any log. Get-WinEvent is the newer, faster cmdlet and reaches every log, including the application-specific ones.

steps.prompt: See what's using the CPU: list the top 5 processes by CPU time.
steps.explanation: SQL Server has used the most CPU time; w3wp is an IIS worker process.
steps.why: This is the object pipeline at work: Get-Process emits process objects, Sort-Object orders them by a property, Select-Object takes five. No awk, no column counting, and the same three cmdlets work on any kind of object. That one idea is what's worth learning about PowerShell.

steps.prompt: The application can't reach its database. Test whether this server can connect to db-1 on port 1433.
steps.fake_output:
ComputerName     : db-1
RemoteAddress    : 10.0.2.15
RemotePort       : 1433
InterfaceAlias   : Ethernet0
SourceAddress    : 10.0.1.21
TcpTestSucceeded : False
steps.explanation: The name resolves, and the TCP connection to port 1433 fails.
steps.why: Test-NetConnection is 'nc -zv' with DNS resolution thrown in: here the name is fine and the port isn't reachable, which sends you to firewalls or the SQL Server service, not to DNS. The refused-versus-timeout reasoning from Networking applies unchanged; add '-InformationLevel Detailed' to see which.

steps.prompt: The same check is needed on all four web servers. Run 'Get-Service W3SVC' on web-1, web-2, web-3, and web-4 at once.
expected_commands: Invoke-Command -ComputerName web-1, web-2, web-3, web-4 -ScriptBlock { Get-Service W3SVC }
steps.fake_output:
Status   Name    DisplayName                        PSComputerName
------   ----    -----------                        --------------
Stopped  W3SVC   World Wide Web Publishing Service  web-1
Running  W3SVC   World Wide Web Publishing Service  web-2
Running  W3SVC   World Wide Web Publishing Service  web-3
Running  W3SVC   World Wide Web Publishing Service  web-4
steps.why: PowerShell remoting (WinRM) is Windows's SSH: Invoke-Command runs a block on many machines in parallel and labels each result with its source, and Enter-PSSession gives an interactive shell. Knowing it's one server out of four changes the diagnosis from 'a bad deploy' to 'something local to web-1'. Ansible manages Windows hosts through the same channel.
